This might be the only game I've ever played where you can shoot mobsters, enraged ducks, mutated poodles, zombie gardeners, rednecks with shotguns, and clowns. Yes, actual clowns, all in a 1920s mansion, right alongside goofy maids who punch you in the face. The game knows it's goofy and fully embraces it—and honestly, I wouldn’t have it any other way.

I've always believed that mid-tier games should be prioritized for remastering, and [i]Killing Time: Resurrected[/i] is proof of this. Finally, one of the 3DO's hidden gems is playable—and, more importantly, enjoyable. Gone are the extremely low FPS and blurry FMVs. What was once a rough experience has been polished with care, allowing it to finally shine. Not blindingly, mind you, but enough to make for a fun afternoon. The fact that Nightdive took the time to combine the best features from all versions shows their love for gaming and dedication to quality. The amount of care poured into such an obscure title speaks for itself.

It’s not going to change your life, and it’s unlikely to become a favorite, but sometimes that's all you need: a game that doesn’t take itself too seriously and is purely focused on being entertaining. There’s a certain charm in its "bit off more than we could chew" vibe that adds to the experience. It’s as if the developers knew they were being overly ambitious but decided to go for it anyway. Sure, they missed more than they hit, but that’s hardly a deal-breaker. I had fun, and if you’re reading this and considering buying the game, you probably will too.

This title is a reminder that they just don’t make games like this anymore—which, to be honest, might be for the best. Yet a part of me still wishes developers today were as adventurous with their creations. For now, though, [i]Killing Time: Resurrected[/i] scratches that '90s FMV madness itch I didn’t even know I had.

[b]TL;DR:[/b] It’s [i]Doom[/i] meets [i]The 7th Guest[/i], and it’s fun. Don’t overthink it; just enjoy it for what it is. Kudos to Nightdive for remastering these mid-tier games that most people have forgotten. Time capsules like this deserve preservation, and Nightdive is doing important work with these remasters.

Maybe [i]Realms of the Haunting[/i] will be next... If [i]Killing Time[/i] made the cut, there’s hope.

I had this for my 3DO back in the day, a Panasonic FZ-1 actually that I stupidly sold at a game store many years ago. Anyway, Killing Time was basic, good fun back in the day at about 3 FPS. The FMV was blocky as hell. It ran at about 1 FPS no matter what. It was almost like playing a tile-based dungeon crawler. That didn't matter though. The atmosphere was top-notch. The enemies were fun and different from anything else that came before. The music was awesome. And every single time I booted it up, I watched the entire intro cinematic. Why? Because it was f'ing cool when I was 13 years old! Now I'm 42 and I'll continue to watch that intro, thank you very much. I look forward to getting further into this remaster. The ability to look around like a modern shooter is splendid! It might not be to everyone's taste, but for those that have the nostalgia for it or just want to try something unique from the past, then this is a pretty fun way to start. Honestly, it's probably worth the $20 without having to worry too much about it. It's just a fun game!

I remember playing Killing Time on the 3DO, where it ran at less than 15 frames per second, with cumbersome controls. Thankfully, this remaster greatly improves gameplay, controls, graphics, and frame rate. This remastered version blends the PC version’s level layout with the 3DO version’s enemy and weapon sprites, now in HD. The PC version allows players to explore both the entire island and the house, while the 3DO version was limited to the manor. 

For those unfamiliar, Killing Time is an open-world first-person shooter with no loading screens. Unlike Doom, the levels are interconnected, gradually revealing mysteries through interactions with the ghosts of the island’s cursed inhabitants. The unique atmosphere, combined with distinctive visuals and music, creates a haunting experience.

The gameplay is fast-paced, featuring a variety of visually striking enemies, secrets, and puzzles. Its Metroidvania-style progression means certain areas remain locked until you find specific magical items, allowing for further exploration. The game also offers multiple endings, enhancing its replay value.

Overall, Killing Time was an ambitious title, and thanks to Night Dive Studios, it’s still a blast to play today. I’m grateful for the HD graphics, smoother gameplay, and restored content that makes this the definitive version. The remaster is truly impressive, and I highly recommend it to anyone seeking an old-school classic.

The beyond-obscure Killing Time by Studio 3DO was the last game I thought Nightdive Studios would ever tackle in a proper remaster, as there are so many more-popular and lauded old 90's and early 00's FPS games that I figured the general buying public would like to see first; but I am so very glad I am wrong. I've always thought this game was treated very unfairly by the passage of time, being developed as a 1st-party exclusive for the 3DO, the first 32-bit CD-ROM 3D-focused game console released, a system that technically never had 1st party hardware, and didn't have 1st party software when launched because the whole point was to be a shared technological standard like VHS was. 

The even more-obscure PC version of this game was a completely different and arguably better game, more fully-realized; but as people found out when it got a port to Steam by IP owners Ziggurat, a game not without its glaring flaws It took a fan-made patch to get the original right for modern Steam users; and even then, there were problems due to the game's original CDROM dependency and the fact it was made in an era before hardware acceleration. There has never been any official patches, so the only commercially-available way to play Killing Time until Nightdive came along was fundamentally broken out of the box, like the abandonware it once was before Ziggurat picked it up. 

Killing Time deserved better, but not enough people cared, so I never expected it to actually get any sort of justice in that regard, until now. If you want to learn more about the specifics of the original PC game, read my review on it I left there, as the rest of this review is about the differences between the remaster and the original. First thing's first, everything that was broken about the original Windows 95 PC release is fixed here in the remaster, full stop. The rest of the changes made to Killing Time via this remaster are aesthetic and gameplay tweaks to address flaws with the original game's execution, not technical hangups from being a PC game from 30 years ago. Nightdive smoothed out the wrinkles, and did a restomod on the engine using KEX.

The original game used a version of the "frankensteined" Doom engine, made from code Carmack wrote for the Atari Jaguar 64, with "Burger" Becky Heineman's BurgerLib to make it run Doom on the 3DO's 32-bit environment. This engine could therefore run directly under Windows 95 instead of needing DOS as Doom did. Now the whole thing is running smooth and up to 120fps in 4K under KEX. Beyond that, Nightdive chose to use the superior photo-captured actor sprites for enemies, weapons, and objects found in the 3DO version of the game, that the PC version couldn't handle due to sprite size limitations the PC had, even though it could render bigger, more complex level geometry. 

This "best of both worlds" means you get the larger, more-detailed, and frankly more-fun PC game, using the sprite assets of the 3DO game, which had better sprite and video capabilities from its custom hardware than what PCs had at the time. Killing Time Resurrected is still the same insane hybrid of "metroidvania" branching non-linear level design on what is basically an open island estate, mixed with Sam Raimi-inspired horror comedy, an Art Deco look a decade before Bioshock did it, in-game storytelling (before Half-Life) through the FMV "apparitions" that appear throughout the world, and madcap mixture of ambient, jazz, ragtime, and opera music often performed by a real band. 

In a rare stroke of luck, most of the original texture, video, audio, and sprite assets in their full resolution were available to Nightdive, thanks to old developers basically keeping all this stuff somewhere on old hard drives, floppy discs, and CD-ROMs, meaning the sprites and textures look uncannily high-resolution, even for a remaster. Seeing 3DO version's live actors in costumes used for the enemies and gun sprites move and fire in near-photorealistic detail, alongside environment textures that are either straight-up photographs or painted on, is a real treat. Combined with the proto survival-horror gameplay where all enemies and items are finite, and the usual run-and-gun Doom-style action, and this is one hell of a sleeper I'm glad more people will now get to experience. 

Nightdive also made some changes to the level design itself that may feel controversial to some, but in my opinion was sorely needed. Many areas (especially inside the mansion) seem copy-pasted with clusters of samey tightly-packed rooms and narrow hallways, probably done in a hurry to meet a deadline, or thought to make combat more challenging by adding claustrophobia or jump scares as you literally run past enemies squeezed into these spaces. Nightdive used original concepts to re-do some of these spaces, removing clusters of rooms and replacing them with more-open areas that have furniture, kitchen counters with more space to walk between, and still fit it all within the same footprint of the original maps.

Other areas actually increased in complexity as some of the copy-paste room design made entire areas skippable as there was nothing there but another room like the one you just passed, as was the case with several of the cave and tomb areas outside the mansion, or in the sewers beneath. Again, levels were tweaked to be more varied, navigable, while still having the same footprint; they even added a cut area called the Bathouse of Osiris, and relocated the cave network that was there to a different part of the map. Some of the crueler puzzles or jumping sections were removed or redone, and a vault of unearthed development goodies were tacked on. I'd say this is the definitive version of Killing Time as we should have always had it, and not your typical "boomer shooter", which is what I've always loved about it.

Killing Time is a remaster of a Doom engine game that was initially stuck on the 3DO (I think there was a Windows port too but it had some issues as well). What sets this apart from other Doom engine games and Doom clones of the time is that this is an open world game set in the 1920s (so lots of art deco motifs and 20s gangsters galore) and rather than cartoony sprites of monsters everything here is digitized from real world actors/photos as was briefly the style in the mid 1990s and it also seamlessly incorporates FMV videos of various ghosts into the game world to help tell the story.

In addition to a solid if not exactly groundbreaking roster of weapons (crowbar, pistol, dual pistols, tommy gun, shot gun, molotov cocktail, flamethrower, and a BFG/Ankh Gun), the game also scatters around some various items that you will need to get into parts of the world that are gated off so there is a sense of exploration and worldbuilding that a lot of older FPSs lacked. Load times are just a tiny hiccup when crossing zones (which are quite large) so the whole thing really does feel like one gigantic Doom level. Music is an interesting mix of ambiance and 1920s inspired pieces. It is different but it works.

The touches added by Nightdive are mostly quality of life improvements that are expected for modern games, and the sprites and textures are all greatly enhanced over their original low resolution counterparts so it looks good at higher resolutions. The game really does hold up great both visually and it plays and runs great as well. I haven't run into any bugs or crashes in my four plus hours of play time so far. It also runs well on the Steamdeck. About half of my playtime has been on the Steamdeck and I had no issues.

I'm really having a blast with this one and I'd highly recommend picking this up to support the great job that Nightdive is doing preserving classic and obscure games alike all the while introducing them to a new generation of gamers. Other developers and publishers could learn a thing or two about remasters from Nightdive.

The game world is surprisingly massive with many different areas to explore with its own nooks and crannies. It was honestly kind of overwhelming at first but once you spend a couple of hours exploring you start to get familiar with them. However, some of them have pretty confusing layouts, like [spoiler] Wine Cellar [/spoiler] which was a pain for me to navigate. 

Also, I feel like the [spoiler] Set / Duncan Boss respawns way too quickly, it felt like every couple of seconds he would pop up around a corner while I was trying to navigate the mansion destroying those final artifacts, thankfully the guy wasn't hard to kill [/spoiler].

Killing Time: Resurrected is a remaster of the cult classic FPS Killing Time, combining aspects of both the PC and 3DO version into a new package. The game follows a student as he travels to Ms. Conway's mysterious abandoned estate island and it's up to them to discover the secrets of what happened on the island and fighting whatever stands in their way.  The game is another early example of a FPS Game with Metroidvania-like elements, though more so in level progression than something like the Remake of Powerslave. 

Gameplay of Killing Time is surprisingly very Doom-y, this might be because the game originally ran in a modified Doom Engine so gameplay quirks from that game more or less apply here. The Player character is given a handful of weapons to defend themselves such as a Crowbars, Knifes, Pistols, Tommy Guns, Shotguns, the works. The more notable weapons of the arsenal are the fire based weapons being a flamethrower and one if the the earliest appearance of a Molotov Cocktail. As well as an weaponized Ankh, the BFG weapon of the game. It's a simple handful of weapons, more so for the fact they only have a primary fire. This won't provide a issue as for the most part a lot of the enemies mirror the same handful of enemy archetypes.  For example, you have enemies that will try to hit you with a hitscan attack, or foes that throw projects, and even ones that try to get close to attack in melee range. The main gameplay loop of the game is exploring around the mansion's ground looking for keys to unlock more areas to explore. The game then becomes more open ended as you are somewhat free to explore to find the large amount of keys and the equally large amount of Urns for completion. While the shooting isn't too complex and the exploration fairly easy for the most part, it's a fun romp around especially for another reason:

Style Wise, Killing Time is a textbook example of the glorious era of the 90s where everyone was using renders and FMV in harmony to create video game graphics. Resurrected does this tenfold as Nightdive took the FMV footage from both the 3DO and PC version. Upscaled digitally and remastered by hand, FMV graphics have never looked better, and easily make's the game stand out because of this art direction. Really the only clashing elements is when the prerendered enemies are mixed in since they're obviously less detailed in comparison. The music is also all over the place in the best way possible, you could have some legitimately ominous and creepy ambience but then walk into a different room and get hit in the face with the most upbeat jazz tunes you've ever heard. It's such a shame that the OST isn't purchasable separate or uploaded elsewhere cause it's really good.

One thing to note is this game much like the Quake II, Dark Forces, and the recent Doom Remasters. Killing Time; Resurrected comes with a vault filled to the brim with cut content, early concepts, and just all the stuff that makes game development really interesting to read into. It's really charming to take a gander in, especially with all the studio footage of the actors for the FMV enemies. You can tell it must have been really fun to make a game like this. You also have a music player in the vault but unfortunately as mentioned there's currently no way officially outside the game to listen to it.

Overall, Killing Time: Resurrected is a fantastic remaster for otherwise a game I doubt any other studio would have dared making a remaster of, let alone one of this quality. While it is a pretty pricy remaster considering the average playthrough is around 3.5-4 hours, you're definitely purchasing a premium for a incredibly high quality product. Hopefully this remaster does well enough to invoke more obscure FPS games the Nightdive Remaster treatment, cause there ain't anyone else who does it with the same level of passion and love for videogame preservation (Plus the original PC version is still available to buy!)

I played this game knowing nothing about the original, and I have to say, it holds up amazingly well.  It's a solid FMV adventure game combined with an equally-solid old-school shooter.

The main selling point of this game is the FMV "cutscenes" that play out in the world via digitized sprites.  It's such a simple and clever trick, allowing story beats to play naturally in-world, that I'm amazed I've never seen another shooter of the era attempt it.  Being able to walk around during story sequences with full control almost makes the game feel like the missing link on the way to more story-based shooters like Half-Life and Bioshock.  It really has to be seen to be believed.

But that's not the game's only feat.  Killing Time features an (almost) seamless open world, with an impressive size for the time.  There's an entire island to explore with plenty of secrets and shortcuts to discover.  The refusal to break the world into separately-loaded chunks also gives the game a surprising amount of persistence.  Any enemy you kill stays dead for the rest of the game, so as you clear out the mansion you get a genuine sense of progression as you're able to safely stroll through hallways that had you fighting for your life just a couple hours ago.

Speaking of fighting, the difficulty is fair.  I played on Normal and found the whole thing pretty breezy.  Clearly, they designed this game with the intention of attracting non-shooter fans who might be enticed by the innovative storytelling.  Or maybe the game's just a lot easier with modern mouselook controls.  Who can say?

My only real point of complaint is the game's save system.  This is one of those games where, whenever you save, you're basically making a save-state that records EVERYTHING exactly as it was.  Unfortunately, this means that if you...say...clip somewhere you shouldn't and can't escape, you can't save-and-load your way back to safety, and indeed attempting to do so will create a save where you're trapped forever.  Killing Time isn't an especially buggy game, but I did have the afore-mentioned scenario happen to me precisely once (thankfully, pretty early on).

If you play this game, definitely see it through to the end.  Without spoilers, the final challenge of the game is easily one of its coolest sequences, leveraging the strengths of the game's open world design in a very clever way.

I highly recommend Killing Time Resurrected even if you have know nostalgia or even knowledge of the original.  It's an amazing hidden gem of the 90s and this is a pitch-perfect update for modern audiences.  Just in time for Halloween, too!

It’s a remarkable boom shoot, despite the cruft of its design. Remarkable, first for its eye-catching digitized sprites. These are some of the cleanest, smoothest digitized sprites I’ve seen in a game and it gives it quite the distinctive look for an old timey fps. I think the level design is also pretty remarkable too, just one large island to wander around in, no load screens, no direction markers. This is also a flaw, with a ton of wandering and backtracking happening until you get a sense of the place, but it’s definitely awe-inspiring to just keep going and going. It sprawls. The enemies are varied, though their behavior not quite so. The typical scenario is to wander into some new area, clear out the dozens upon dozens of enemies, and then scope out the map. Thankfully, the environs and variety of enemies keep things engaging even as you backtrack and blast over and over. The final thing I find remarkable is how they conveyed the story. Instead of cutscenes, you wander upon “ghosts” that, upon staying stationary in front of, load up a green-screened actor that proceeds to play out a scene floating right on top of the gameplay area. You can move around and even be interrupted by enemies while these scenes play out, and there’s nothing quite like it out there. For its flaws, the short length and unique features make it well worth trying out and I’m glad NightDive preserved and improved it for our enjoyment today.

KT itself might not be nothing much itself. As I mentioned, it is perhaps the only open world FPS of the era, forcing you to explore, backtrack and collect items in order to gain access to new places. It's not particuraly hard, actually it's pretty easy, even in higher difficulties, this is not a challenging game, and it boasts a particular sense of humour that is akin to the crummy FMV times of the SEGA CD, when everything seemed to go into fully acted and digitalized performers mixed up in interactive movies. This seemed the way of the future at the time, believe it or not.

Maybe the fact that this is essentialy a 3DO affair is what took it into obscurity in the first place, but something that was probably a rather forgetable characteristic of a crummy FPS bound to be buried into oblivion boasts nowadays some very interesting, fun and aesthetic bunch of qualities. In the age we are living now, of retro gaming and nostalgia trips. in which different games are trying to replicate the nostalgia of the 90's, Killing Time is a gem to be discovered. Killing Time was a revelation when it first came out. It was the first game I ever played with a fully interconnected open world and absolutely zero loading screens. The whole game is structured like an FPS Metroidvania, which was incredibly unique for its time and, honestly, still feels fresh and distinct even today.

The atmosphere, music, and those distinct digitized FMV enemies gave the original 3DO version a vibe unmatched by anything else. However, this remaster creates a bit of a weird situation. While it includes the high-res 3DO sprites, it mixes them with 3D renders from the PC version. This results in a clash of styles—a visual mishmash that somewhat ruins the game's overall aesthetic consistency.

There is also one big piece of the puzzle missing. I personally prefer the original 3DO map layout (which focused on a larger, more complex mansion) over the PC layout used here.

Verdict: The devs have stated that the proper 3DO version will be added soon via a mod. Once that happens—unifying the style and restoring the original map—this will undeniably be the Ultimate Release. For now, without it, it feels slightly incomplete. Despite that, it is still a fantastic resurrection of a one-of-a-kind classic. Highly recommended, but keep an eye out for that mod!

Clicked play on my Steam, never heard of this beforehand, but some of my friends had wishlisted this and it looked silly enough to warrant my attention, so when it released, I put down the 19 bucks on the counter, spread my arms wide and said "surprise me." The first thing that greeted me was delicious FMV, the kind of shit your Grandma cooks up in the kitchen, homemade, made with love type shit. So already, Killing Time has given me a plate of memories and FMV sweets. The flavors of Realms of the Haunting and Disruptor melt over my tongue and mouth like a bonbon. Rev up a new game, clicked on Very Hard (still loathe resurrecting enemies) and began the game. Looking on the Steam page, I expected tongue-in-cheek humor, silly and fun. Hell, we have tickling clowns with their giant hands going up to the player's face like it was an OneyPlays bit. The last thing I would’ve expected was the player character standing alone on a boat, water lazily lapping against the wood, waves in the distant crash against the cliff sides, just you, Mother Sea, and the sounds of Heaven’s tones. The first track of the game is ethereal bliss. The choirs of Father God sing for you and in this moment, for you alone. What can only be described as Vangelis’ protege, soundscapes of blue skies, worn skin, and peace echo on the small dock. I simply close my eyes and bask in this. I’m already floored. I walk into the nearby building and two people from the past walk onto the stage, spotlights on them. Duncan and Mike discuss some unsavory business, arms, bootlegging. The long arm of the law being used to dig into the pockets of America to rob her blind. “Okay, I’m in, what else does this game got?” Go up stairs to be greeted by the fucking Blowjob Brothers with shitty New Yorker accent mowing me down with Tommy Guns and missing every shot except the one that grazes me and does like 10 points of damage. From here, I’m forever locked in. The silly mixed with the genuinely tense atmosphere and every single other aspect in-between. Killing Time is a pretty solid FPS game brimming with charm and glee for itself. Nothing too crazy, just a good time.

As someone who already 100% the game and got all the achievements on it, I gotta admit, this might be my favorite way of playing Killing Time nowadays.
Now, don't get me wrong, I played the original PC version and it was almost serviceable, but as someone who played the 3DO version first and absolutely loved the real-life actors used even as enemy sprites, the wooden crates that you can either loot or use as weapons, the mazy yet enjoyable state layout or even the secrets and hidden paths to whole other areas from above, the original PC version was, in a way, a step down for me, specially since it felt like a less impactful or creative experience and they could've kept the new enemies and weapons, while somehow keeping the old map design.
Yeah I know the 3DO version barely hold its framerate, but the map exploration was still enjoyable, and even the shooting considering the kind of hardware it was on.
Now, how does this remaster holds up?
Well, I can say from the get go that, luckily, a lot of the annoying level design from the PC version was altered in order to improve here. Narrow halways are replaced or were made wider, obnoxious puzzles are either easened up or outright removed which makes the game flow even better, and now the Knife, an unfinished 3DO weapon, finally made its stellar debut here.
I was at first skeptical of Nightdive choosing the PC map as the base here, but to be honest, playing through the PC map with all the enhancements and the improved level design made me appretiate it more. Even if I miss the 3DO layout for as confusing as it can be at first, this game is still an amazing rendition to the best content out of both versions, and, as a FPS, it holds up really well too, since ammo can get real tight if you're shooting a lot without giving that much thought.
The soundtrack is also one of my favorite parts, yeah, the original Circus Mortus song from the 3DO is still used outdoors and not with clowns here for... some reason, but when you see stuff like the included Vault on the main menu to show some development history, the high resolution scans of the sprites, and even the PC enemies that weren't on the original 3DO version getting remade from the ground up for this remaster, you have what, after Powerslave Exhumed, is my favorite Nightdive's niche 90s FPS remaster.

As a kid in 1997, I easily convinced my parents to get me a 3DO and a slew of games with it.. was real easy as the 3DO had been discontinued and everything was at bargain bin prices. This included a long box version of Kiilling Time. It's badly worn now from use. Otherwise it'd be worth more than a hundred bucks now on Ebay!

I remembered looking at the box inserts on my way home, including the protagonist Hargrove's 'handwritten' map of the estate, thinking what an awesome game this would be. When I got around to playing it, the FMV opening (the same as the one here) and the opening theme instantly got me hooked. 

And then I started playing it. I didn't understand why it was just so damn difficult. I could never play it without the easily accessible invincible mode. It was the horrible framerate. I still played it a number of times- always on cheat and I loved it. For some strange reason though, the original 3DO version only featured a bad ending. 

Released in 1995 at the time the 32-bit 3DO was on its last legs and poorly poised to compete with the then-upcoming Sega and Sony 32 bit consoles, 3DO put on their developer hat- Studio 3DO, and released some of the best games for the systems. This was one of the best at least for its original storyline, soundtrack, and the creative way it incorporated FMV elements at a time when FMV games where basically just interactive movies with videos.

I've not played the 1996 PC port but this game definitely does the original justice. It fixes the main issue- the horrible framerate.. on hindsight, this is probably why the developers made invisibility so easily accessible.. they know how impossible hard it was. It improves the maps too.

(mild spoilers ahead)
I wish the maps could be made yet more intuitive. I often got lost in the sprawling outdoor areas, wondering which paths I've taken, and those damn levers! I went around it circles trying to find those damn little things that open up the paths you need to advance. Also the power-up amulets etc were never useful- they activate upon collection and when you usually get to them in an area, you'd usually have defeated most of the enemies there.

Overall, as someone who spent hours on the original, this gives Killing Time the justice it deserves. I sure hope they release the OST on Spotify. It's still spooky and awesome as ever.

Pretty cool Doom clone from back in the day. I like that it takes place in one large seamless world with lots of key-hunting and backtracking, but it can get really confusing if you don't write down where the color-coded doors are and which areas you've already gotten the required ancient artifacts from. The overhead map is almost entirely worthless and the game really doesn't give you much direction on where to go. 

Level design is decent, but a bit too maze-like, and the game's atmosphere is really inconsistent. One moment you'll have characters that fit the theme like the undead gangsters and demon dogs, accompanied by some really creepy Doom 64-esque ambient music, and then the next you'll be fighting clowns with silly upbeat music playing. Some of the enemy types like the flying red faces and generic Halloween skeletons are very low-effort and not at all scary. The weapon selection is just okay - you'll be using the shotgun and flamethrower for most of it, which makes the experience rather repetitive. This game is also extremely easy on the medium setting - tons of ammo and health pickups are thrown at you, and the hitscan enemies like the gangsters shoot like Stormtroopers. 

Where the game succeeds is in its storytelling, with FMV flashbacks of the characters playing as you progress through the mansion, slowly revealing how everything went wrong and who the villain of the story is. The acting is a bit hokey, but enjoyable. Overall this game had potential to be a lot better than it is, but it's still a fun game with an interesting setting. Worth buying on sale.

Nightdive Studios have been releasing a heap of old school games that would otherwise be lost to time and making them (in most cases) compatible with modern hardware and software. I've come across both old favourites from my childhood as well as discovered hidden gems I never knew about in their library of titles.

However, for me it clashed something intruigingly with my PC setup in a way I've never had a game do before. The longer a session I played, the more delayed my shooting became. I would click and click, and it didn't register, but then it seemed to be gathering in a delayed lineup of inputs, so as my guns would seem to auto shoot and wouldn't stop. So, from what I can gather, there was an issue between inputs being registered and then performed by the game. If I stopped the game and then came back to it, it went fine and smooth again, until it racked up in delays and became worse and worse over time again. I have no idea how to describe this phenomenon correctly, I'm sure there is a term for it, maybe input delay stacking, but obviously the games config and/or optimization didn't agree with my PC for whatever reason.

But, when I tried googling this issue, I didn't find anyone else reporting it, so I'm gonna go ahead and give this a positive review considering the love and care for the quality overall that the game has recieved by the Nightdive crew, cleaning up the visuals and adding info and extras that they could find. A remaster of the original Killing Time, Killing Time: Resurrected adds modern controls to the game, as well as a few extra things I won't spoil. I have played the original, but the controls on it are very outdated (and I mean, duh, it's almost thirty years old) so being able to use a mouse and keyboard or even a gamepad makes this game so much more approachable.  

So what is this game about, you may be asking? Your character, who aside from the intro and ending never speaks, is heading to this forgotten by time island to follow up on a mission his Egyptology Professor did. Upon reaching the island, his watch is stopped, he's accosted by various enemies, and he is haunted by the ghostly figure of Tess Conway. Tess wanted eternal life, and let's just say something went horribly wrong. What happened? You need to figure that out while surviving this dangerous island.

Gameplay is an FPS where you need to find keys and parts of Tess' spirit. That's much easier said than done, however. The game barely ever gives you any clues. Once Tess has laid out the mission for you, you're on your own. You get a map which can help, but this game doesn't throw you any bones after meeting Tess on her front lawn. As you walk around, you'll have to get accustomed to Tess saying "Help Me!" You'll be hearing that constantly. You'll find her ghost floating around, and stopping near it will trigger a cutscene, showing some interactions between the island residents before things went to hell. Of course we have Tess but also her faithful Butler Robert, the sleezy Duncan, and a few others. They might give you hints on where to go, but they're very vague.

But you're not alone on this island. You'll constantly be accosted by various enemies. Mobsters, zombies, insects, even clowns! And they will be a constant thorn in your side until you use your weapons to put them down. We're not exactly armed to the teeth here, but the weapons are fun to use.  I fully admit I cheated my way through this game and feel no shame in doing so.  You'll need to find the keys to unlock doors (duh) to access new areas to find the parts of Tess' spirit. Things like her mouth, her nose, her ears, and her chest (yes, you get to hold Tess' chest, her lovely, supple che-*shot*) and a few others. These also give you powers you can use, such as being able to see enemies on the map but I didn't use these that much. 

As I've said, this game is hard to finish, hard to know where you need to go...and that's why I recommend you play it without a guide. It's so satisfying to finally figure out where you need to go after stumbling around for so long.  I robbed myself of that satisfaction by not taking my own advice (and I also spoiled the ending for myself) so I want you to have that so I can vicariously have it through you.

Another great remaster by Nightdive, but that doesn't mean the game is particularly good at all. Killing Time is very of its time, in the sense that it's one of those early horror games that doesn't know what the word "horror" means, sorta like Alone in the Dark. The weapons feel sucky, the 3D0 enemy designs vary from "yeah, that looks alright" to "That's pretty bad". Even the PC characters looked bad. Most of the time, I'm pretty jarred at several of the sound design choices. With 3D0 actors on, the humanoid enemies talk and make annoying noises when shot. There are some enemies, like the hunter/shotgunner who yell, then shoot, but the actual attack happens before the shot fires. Other designs like any of the ghosts are laughably bad in either version of the sprites. They're just floating red heads with some ghostly horned baby things. Looks terrible. I know there could be the excuse made that this is an old game, of course it's going to look bad, but I'd tell you to look at Heretic, Hexen, Necrodome, Duke Nukem 3D, Blood, pretty much any Raven Software or Build Engine game had better sprites. Back on sound, the music also varies from "Yeah, that's alright", like the music in the intro docks, the forest ambience, that's all fine and well, but that's like 3 songs. The rest of the music is obnoxious and has me questioning if whoever the hell the composer is was either doing crack or just rubbing his ass over a synthesizer. An example of this is pretty much any other song in any other area... yeah.

EDIT: I just found out some stuff.

So toggling 3DO actors in menu doesn't just change sprites, it changes character behaviours too, which the PC version was not intended to have at all. In addition to this, not all enemies on PC were on 3DO, which means that not all enemies were remastered, they were just swapped in the "3DO actors" mode. This seriously affects gameplay, because clowns become more annoying with 3DO actors, so do the dogs, the gangsters, the hunters, the harpies, and the wasps/bees. Nightdive, please, if you're going to do a remaster of this scale, please offer the 3DO version of the game in this remaster for one, and please just have a toggle between 3DO actors, remastered 3DO actors, PC actors and remastered PC actors. 

TLDR: Good remaster, questionable game.
